full_judgment:
10. It is also the fundamental principle of criminal jurisprudence that it is always for the prosecution to prove its charge against the accused beyond reasonable doubt and this onus on the prosecution never shifts. In the case of Chan Kau vs R (1955) AC 206 it was held that at common law, every defence except insanity must be negatived by the Crown. McNaughten's Case decided that everyone is presumed to be sane until the contrary is proved. As such, the accused who raises the defence of insanity has the burden of establishing it. The same principle is also highlighted in section 105 of the Evidence Act. Section 105 reads as follows: 

 "105. When a person is accused of any offence, the burden of proving the existence of circumstances bringing the case within any of the general exceptions in the Penal Code, or within any special exception or proviso contained in any other part of the same Code or in any law defining the offence is upon him, and the court shall presume the absence of such circumstances.” 

 20. In the instant case, it was revealed during trial that the accused had a previous history of lunacy for which he was under treatment in various places. Although the prosecution had no burden to establish negatively that the accused was not of unsound mind when he killed the victim but their negligence coupled with failure to uncover his such previous mental illness only highlights their inherent weakness in their investigation in a serious crime like a murder case. The investigation of a crime requires, in all fairness, a thorough and meaningful probing into all sorts of circumstances leading to the commission of the crime, otherwise, injustice is bound to result in many a case. 

 25. It is also well settled since McNaughten's case (1843) that all persons are presumed to be sane and it is for the defence to prove the insanity of the accused at the precise moment when he committed the offence although the initial burden to establish the offence is always on the prosecution who has to prove its allegations against an accused beyond reasonable doubt and such onus on the prosecution never shifts. But in contradistinction to such onus on the prosecution, the burden to prove the insanity, on the part of the defence is not that onerous, the accused is required to prove his plea of insanity on the balance of probabilities on preponderance of evidence. Reliance in this respect may be made in the case of Sodeman vs R (PC) (1936) 2 All ER 1138. Viscount Hailsham, LC held at page 1140 as follows : 

 " it is certainly plain that the burden in cases in which an accused has to prove insanity may fairly be stated as not being higher than the burden which rests upon a plaintiff or defendant in civil proceedings." 

 26. These two categories of burden of proof, one on the prosecution and the other on the accused raising the plea of insanity, are considered by the Supreme Court of India in the case of Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar vs State of Gujarat AIR 1964 (SC) 1563. In the said case, K Subba Rao, J., quoted with approval the treatment of the point by Glanville Williams in his celebrated work 'Criminal Law' in the following manner: 

 "A Scottish case, HM Advocate Vs Fraser (1878) 4 Couper 70, noticed in Glanville Williams' "Criminal Law". The General Part, 2nd Edn., P 517, pinpoints the distinction between these two categories of burden of proof. There, a man killed his baby while he was asleep; he was dreaming that he was struggling with a wild beast. The learned author elaborates the problem thus: 

 "When the Crown proved that the accused had killed his baby what may be called on evidential presumption or presumption of fact arose that the killing was murder. Has no evidence been adduced for the defence the jury could have convicted of murder, and their verdict would have been upheld on appeal. The burden of adducing evidence of the delusion therefore lay on the accused. Suppose that, when all the evidence was in, the jury did not know what to make of the matter. They might suspect the accused to be inventing a tale to cover his guilt, and yet not be reasonably certain about it. In that event the accused would be entitled to an acquittal. the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt not only the actus reus but the mens rea." (Para-6). 

 Subba Rao, J thereafter formulated the legal position on the burden of proof in the context of the plea of insanity in the following manner: 

 "The doctrine of burden of proof in the context of the plea of insanity may be stated in the following propositions: (1) The prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had committed the offence with the requisite mens rea; and the burden of proving that always rests on the prosecution from the beginning to the end of the trial, (2) There is a rebuttable presumption that the accused was not insane, when he committed the crime, in the sense laid down by section 84 of the Indian Penal Code; the accused may rebut it by placing before the court all the relevant evidence-oral, documentary or circumstantial, but the burden of proof upon him is not higher than that rests upon a party to civil proceedings, (3) Even if the accused was not able to establish conclusively that he was insane at the time he committed the offence, the evidence placed before the court by the accused or by the prosecution may raise a reasonable doubt in the mind of the court as regards one or more of the ingredients of the offence, including mens rea of the accused and in that case the court would be entitled to acquit the accused on the ground that the general burden of proof resting on the prosecution was not discharged." (Para-7). 

 27. In view of the above noted facts and circumstances, it appears that the prosecution failed to discharge its burden of proving the case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, rather, there is doubt as to whether he was capable of knowing the nature of his act when he killed the victim Happy Rani Halder and the accused is entitled to the benefit of such a doubt and, as such, we are of the view that the accused is not guilty of the charge under section 302 of the Penal Code and he is entitled to be acquitted.
